title: Jade Agent Stack
subtitle: Driving Jade Vault and Agent Base safely: harness, approvals, playbooks, sites, surfaces and security, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course based on the open Jade Agent Stack toolkit (github.com/lucky-edgelord/jade-agent-stack, MIT). Learn how the Jade parts fit together (Vault asks, Base answers, Base logs, Base can say no); configuration, the OS keyring and header-only authentication; the harness with approval patterns where deny wins, idempotency keys and short-lived task credentials; stable error codes, exit codes and version compatibility; portable YAML playbooks with check, plan, approve, run, rollback and resume; the site compiler from a YAML spec to pages and a Base backend; the CLI, REPL, JSON lines, MCP, HTTP and Python surfaces and how agents work through them; and the threat model with defences against prompt injection. Based on version 0.1.0 of the documentation; check the repository for later changes. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus an approvals tester and a playbook run simulator.

chapters.title: The stack: five parts and one contract

maps.title: Jade stack
links: Kit | embeds | Vault in a page
Stack | is | A client of all four
Contract | says | Base can say no

summary: Jade Agent Stack is one Python package that drives four other Jade repositories: Vault, Agent Base, Agent Kit and Agent UI/UX. It is a client, not a fork, and it speaks to them only through documented interfaces.

The division of labour is summed up in one line: Vault asks, Base answers, Base logs, Base can say no. Vault owns the agent loop and the person's transcript; Base owns identity, the database, the model gateway, billing and the authoritative audit log.
The rules between them are short: tool calls over MCP or REST, one short-lived credential per task, an idempotency key on every mutation, and a refusal means stop and tell the person.

glossary.def: The part that decides and schedules: here Jade Vault, with the agent loop, schedules, approvals and the person.
The part that holds and serves resources: here Jade Agent Base, with identity, database, model gateway, billing and audit log.
The embeddable subset of Vault, an agent in any web page.
A short-lived, least-privilege credential minted for one task.
Base's authoritative record of every tool call and refusal, which agents cannot change.

keyPoints: Vault asks. Base answers. Base logs. Base can say no.
Seam: MCP at /api/agent/mcp, same tools over REST.
Vault owns the transcript; Base owns the audit.
One credential per task, at most 24 h.

items: ELI5. A manager tells the helpers what to do, and a records office keeps the files and writes down every request, even the ones it says no to. If the office says no, the helper stops and tells the person.

Imagine a company with a manager and a records office. The manager decides what to do and talks to people; the records office keeps the files, checks who is allowed to see what, and writes down every request it handles, including the ones it turns down. Jade splits an AI agent system the same way.
Jade Vault is the manager, the control plane. Jade Agent Base is the records office, the resource plane.

Four repositories, and one toolkit over them. Vault runs the agent loop, schedules, the heartbeat, autonomy levels, budgets and approvals, and shows the person the transcript. Base provides identity, the database, the model gateway, billing and the audit log.

Kit is the embeddable subset of Vault, so a web page can host an agent. UI/UX supplies web components and themes. The Stack package is a client over all of them: an SDK, a command line, a setup wizard, a safety harness, portable playbooks and a site compiler. It copies none of their logic.

The seam between Vault and Base is the Model Context Protocol. Base serves tools at its MCP endpoint, and the same tools are available over plain REST. Every tool call carries an authority, a short-lived credential that Vault mints for one task.

Base validates the arguments, checks scopes, runs the call, logs it and answers. If it says no, with a missing scope, a refused credential or a reused idempotency key, the client stops and tells the person; it does not look for a way around.

lesson.code:
# the shape of one call, in pseudocode
cred = vault.mint(task='job-42', scopes=['read', 'write'], ttl='15m')
result = base.call('records_list', {'collection': 'posts'}, credential=cred)
# Base: validate -> check scope -> run -> write agent_audit -> answer
# on 403 credential_refused: stop, tell the person, never retry

items: Because Base keeps the authoritative audit log, even a compromised or confused agent leaves a trail that it cannot edit. Because credentials are short and narrow, a stolen one is worth little. Because Vault owns the transcript, Base never stores conversations on its behalf.
Throughout this course, watch for how each design choice limits the damage a mistaken or manipulated agent can do.

practice.title: Valid TTL
practice.intro: Write ttl_ok(seconds): True if a credential lifetime is at least 1 second and at most 24 hours (86400 seconds).
practice.solution:
def ttl_ok(seconds):

practice.hint: Every call carries a task id.

def audit_for_task(entries, task_id):
    return [[e[1], e[2]] for e in entries if e[0] == task_id]

practice.intro: Write allowed_by_scope(granted, required): True if every required scope is in granted.
practice.solution:
def allowed_by_scope(granted, required):
    return all([r in granted for r in required])

chapters.title: Install, configuration and secrets
summary: Install with pip (Python 3.11 or later, needing only PyYAML). The setup wizard jade init writes jade.config.yaml, and jade doctor checks that every target is reachable, authenticated, compatible and free of tokens in URLs.
The config is found by walking up from the working directory, or from the JADE_CONFIG variable. Unknown keys are errors, and the file never holds secrets.
Secrets are looked up in an order: JADE_SECRET environment variables first (good for CI), then the OS keyring, then an opt-in 0600 file. Tokens travel only in the Authorization header.

glossary.def: The toolkit's configuration file: targets, models, approvals, defaults and routes, with no secrets.
The operating system's secret store, used under the service name jade.
Sending tokens in an Authorization header, never in the URL.
A command that checks configuration, secrets and each target.
A setup wizard that remembers earlier answers and can be restarted or run headless.

keyPoints: A URL with a token is refused.

items: ELI5. Before the helper works, it needs a set of keys. You write where the door is in a notebook, but you never write the key in the notebook.
Getting started takes two commands. After installing the package, jade init walks through seven steps: environment, targets, auth, models, permissions, a smoke test and writing the file.

It is resumable, so an interrupted setup continues where it stopped, and it can run headless with a file of answers or with defaults. Then jade doctor confirms that each target can be reached, that your token works, that versions are compatible and that no token is hiding in a URL.
The configuration file is plain YAML. Under targets you name Base and Vault by URL, plus the keyring name of the token for each. Other keys set model defaults, approvals, call timeouts and routes.

The toolkit finds the file by looking in the working directory and then each parent folder in turn, unless the JADE_CONFIG variable points somewhere. Any key it does not recognise is an error, which catches typos before they silently do nothing.

lesson.code:
# jade.config.yaml (no secrets here)
version: 1
targets:
  base:
    url: https://base.example.com
    token: jade.base.example.com      # the keyring name, not the token
    credentials: {ttl: 15m, enabled: true}
  vault:
    url: http://127.0.0.1:8099
approvals:
  base.read: ["*"]
defaults: {timeout: 30, chat_timeout: 300}

items: Secrets deserve more care than settings. The lookup order is environment variables named JADE_SECRET followed by the upper-cased secret name, then the OS keyring under the service jade, and finally a file with mode 0600 that you must opt into.
The jade secret commands set, list names of and remove secrets, and never print values.

Tokens go in the Authorization header; a URL containing a token, which would end up in logs and browser history, is refused by the client and by the local server, and a Vault that still accepts a token in the query string is refused as well.

Every one of these choices is about keeping secrets out of places where they leak: files committed to version control, shell histories, log lines and error messages. Output and errors are redacted of registered secrets.
The habit to take away is that configuration describes where things are, and secrets are only ever fetched at the moment of use.

chapters.title: The harness: approvals, idempotency and task credentials

maps.title: Harness
links: Task credential | limits | Scope and time

summary: Every SDK call and command passes through the harness before it leaves, in the same process. It applies approvals, attaches idempotency keys and mints short-lived credentials.

Approvals are patterns by capability and target, such as base.write: record_*:bookings. Deny rules win over allow rules. A call that no rule covers needs a person to confirm, and destructive tools need confirmation even when allowed.
Mutations always carry an idempotency key, so a retry cannot run twice. Task credentials last minutes and carry only the scopes the task needs; a refusal stops the run.

glossary.def: The in-process layer that checks every call: approvals, idempotency, credentials and compatibility.
A pattern permitting or denying a capability on a target, where deny always beats allow.
An identifier ensuring a mutation runs once; a repeat gets the first answer.
A short-lived token with limited scopes minted for one task.
A flag that skips confirmation, always recorded in the approvals log.

items: ELI5. A guard at the door has a list. If a name is on the 'no' list, that is final, even if it is also on the 'yes' list. Names on neither list get a question to a grown-up.

Think of the harness as a security desk at the door of a building. Every call, whether from a script, an agent or a person at the command line, must pass it. The desk consults a list of what is permitted. If an entry denies the visitor, that settles it.
If nothing mentions the visitor, a person is asked. Only if an entry allows the visit does it go ahead without asking, and even then the desk insists on a signature for anything destructive.
The list is the approvals section of the config. Each key names a capability: base.read, base.write, base.schema and other Base scopes, vault.chat, vault.flow, kit.page, shell, http_request.

Each value lists target patterns where star matches anything, like record_star colon bookings meaning any record tool on the bookings collection. A deny rule always wins, even over a broader allow. A bare true is rejected as too vague.
Every confirmation, refusal and use of the yolo flag is appended to a local approvals log with the time, target, task and scope.
Idempotency is the second safeguard. A mutation always carries a key: one you give, one from a context manager, or a fresh UUID. Base runs a given key once and replays the first answer for 24 hours.
So if a phone sleeps mid-flow, or a network drops after the request arrived, sending it again is safe. The same key with different arguments is a conflict, error JADE205.
Reads may retry on network errors; mutations never retry on their own, because the toolkit cannot know whether the first attempt happened.

The third safeguard is the task credential. A with-block over a task mints a Base credential, valid fifteen minutes by default, scoped to what the task needs, and revokes it afterwards. Even a hijacked task cannot do more than its scopes allow, and not for long.

If Base answers credential_refused the run stops and is not retried. Compatibility is checked as well: a major version mismatch with a target is refused. Together, approvals limit what may be asked, keys limit repeats, and credentials limit power.

chapters.title: Errors, exit codes and version compatibility
summary: Every failure has a stable code of the form JADE and three digits, a message and a remediation. The first digit groups them: 1xx auth and secrets, 2xx remote, 3xx safety, 4xx user input, 5xx doctor.
Exit codes tell scripts what kind of failure it was: 0 ok, 1 user error, 2 remote error, 3 refused for safety. A script should treat 3 as a stop, not something to retry.
Version checks keep the parts compatible: a different major version is refused (JADE203), an older minor is a warning. A Vault that accepts tokens in URLs is refused (JADE102).

glossary.def: An identifier that never changes meaning, so tools can react to it.
A sentence telling the reader how to fix the problem.
The number a command returns to the shell: 0 success, nonzero failure.
The first number of a version; a change means incompatible interfaces.
The health check comparing target versions with STACK.md.

keyPoints: Major mismatch refused, older minor warns.

items: ELI5. Each job gets a ticket number. If you hand in the same ticket twice, the shop does the job once and just shows you the first answer again.

Good error handling is half of good automation. Jade's errors have codes that never change meaning, such as JADE100 for not configured or JADE301 for denied by approvals, a human message, and a remediation sentence.

Printing an error shows all three, and never a secret, because messages pass through redaction. In Python they all derive from one class, JadeError, carrying the code, message, remediation and exit code.

The codes are grouped. The hundreds digit says where to look. JADE1xx concerns authentication and secrets: no config, a bad token, a refused legacy URL-token Vault, a refused credential, a missing secret store or secret.

JADE2xx concerns the remote target: unreachable, protocol mismatch, an error answer, an incompatible version, a timeout, an idempotency conflict. JADE3xx is safety: approval required, denied, unsafe without confirmation, playbook not approved.
JADE4xx is bad input: invalid config, playbook or site spec, unknown or ambiguous tool, not found, stale generated files. JADE500 means doctor failed.

Scripts see the same classification as exit codes. Zero is success. One is your mistake: fix the input. Two is the remote side: it may be down, so a read can be retried later. Three is a refusal for safety: approvals, credentials, or an unapproved playbook.
A wrapper script must treat three as final. Retrying around a refusal is exactly the behaviour the design tries to prevent.

Versions are the other source of trouble, so the toolkit declares what it works with in STACK.md: Base from 0.6.0, Vault from 2.18.3, Kit from 3.1.0 and UI from 1.2.0 in version 0.1.0. Doctor compares what each target reports.

A different major version is refused, since interfaces changed incompatibly. An older minor version only warns. Because JADE102 treats a Vault that still accepts tokens in query strings as unsafe, a too-old Vault is refused for security reasons as well.

chapters.title: Playbooks: portable automation

maps.title: Playbooks
links: Fail mode | decides | What happens next
Approval | binds | To a file hash

summary: A playbook is a YAML file of tasks that compile to the targets' existing primitives: Base tools, Vault's HTTP API, a Kit page and local commands. You check it, plan it, approve it and run it.

Each task can register its result, run only when a condition holds, retry, and declare an undo. Three failure modes decide what a failed task does: stop, continue, or roll back by running undos in reverse.
Runs are resumable and idempotent. Approval is bound to the SHA-256 of the file, so any edit needs a new approval, and unattended runs require it.

glossary.def: A YAML file with apiVersion jade/v1, kind Playbook, metadata and a spec of ordered tasks.
A listing of every call a playbook would make, produced without making any.
A failure mode that runs each finished task's undo in reverse order and then stops.
Saving a task's result under a name for later tasks to use.
A sandboxed template such as double braces around a name, with no calls, imports or I/O.

keyPoints: Rollback needs undo on mutating tasks.
Key = hash of playbook, task and vars.
Edit the file, lose the approval.

items: ELI5. When something breaks the system says a code number and what to do about it. A code beginning with three means 'I stopped on purpose, do not try to sneak past'.

When you do the same set-up twice, write it down. A playbook is that written-down procedure, in YAML, made safe to run. Its spec lists targets, optional scopes for a short-lived credential, variables, defaults and tasks. Each task names a tool and arguments, or a local command, or a block of tasks.
It does not replace Vault's own flows or Jade Lisp; it compiles down to primitives they already understand.

Because playbooks change real systems, there is a ritual. Check validates the file against the schema, and arguments against each tool's own schema; unknown keys are errors. Plan lists every call, with secrets as placeholders, and makes none. Approve signs the SHA-256 of the file with a local key.
Run executes. Edit one character and the hash changes and the approval lapses. Unattended runs through MCP or HTTP need that approval; interactive runs ask you.
Failure handling is explicit. In stop mode a failed task ends the run, which is the default. In continue mode the run goes on, useful for checks such as is it there already.

In rollback mode, each finished task's undo runs in reverse order and then the run stops; check refuses a rollback playbook whose mutating tasks lack an undo. Blocks have rescue and always lists, like try and finally. Tasks can retry up to ten times, or repeat until a condition is true.
Every mutating call gets an idempotency key, by default a hash of the playbook name, task name and variables, so running again is safe. The run state is recorded locally.

If a phone sleeps or a network breaks, running again with the same variables resumes: finished tasks are skipped, unfinished ones are sent with the same keys, and Base replays anything that had already arrived.
Expressions in arguments use a small sandboxed language with comparisons, and, or, not, in, and a few filters like default, lower and length. An unknown name is an error unless a default is given.

chapters.title: Sites: one YAML file to a website and its backend
summary: A site is one file, jade.site.yaml, compiled to static HTML that loads the Agent UI/UX components. A name, a tagline and a template make a whole site; the same spec can also configure the Base backend with collections, sign-in, models, plans and billing.

Eight templates, twelve themes and nineteen sections give the building blocks. Pages in the spec replace the template's page at the same path, and backend lists merge by name. A settled design can be saved as a reusable template.
Deploying is a generated playbook, so approvals, idempotency keys, task credentials and resumption all apply. Plan first: it lists every Base call and makes none.

glossary.def: The YAML description of a site: name, tagline, template, theme, pages and backend.
A starting set of pages and backend defaults that the spec can override.
A page building block such as nav, hero, features, pricing or form.
The part of the spec that sets up Base: modules, auth, collections, models, plans and billing.
A compact text form for collection fields, such as email:email! for a required email.

keyPoints: Merge by name, replace by path.

items: ELI5. A recipe card lists steps. You read it first, ask for a pretend run, get a grown-up to sign it, then cook. If a step fails, you undo the earlier steps backwards, like unstacking blocks.

The idea is a compiler for websites. You write three lines, a name, a tagline and a template, and the compiler produces pages. Pages become folders with an index file, so slash pricing becomes pricing/index.html, and there is a 404 page, a sitemap and a robots file.
Everything loads the UI components from a pinned CDN address. Every piece of text is escaped, and markdown drops raw HTML and javascript links, so a spec cannot smuggle script into a page.

lesson.code:
name: Acme AI
tagline: Embeddings for every app.
template: saas
url: https://acme.example.com
pages:
  - path: /
    sections:
      - nav
      - {type: hero, title: "Search that understands"}
      - {type: form, collection: waitlist, fields: ["email:email!"], submit: Join}
      - footer
backend:
  collections:
    - {name: waitlist, fields: "email:email!", create: anyone, list: admin}

items: Templates and specs combine by simple rules. A page in your spec replaces the template's page with the same path. Lists in the backend, such as collections, providers, models and plans, merge by name, so you can adjust one plan without restating them all.

Templates are searched in your project, then your own folder, then the built-in ones, and a template may build on another. Once a design is just right, jade site template save keeps it, and a new site becomes name, tagline and template: house.
Collections have a compact field language: a name, a colon and a type, an exclamation mark for required, separated by commas.
The access rules come as words: anyone means open, users means signed in, owner means the record's owner (it adds a user relation), and admin means no rule, so only superusers.
Each backend key becomes a Base tool call: module_enable, auth_provider_set, collection_create, provider_set, model_set, plan_set, billing_setup and plan_publish.
Deploy is where the earlier chapters pay off. Plan prints the calls as a list with secret placeholders; secrets come from environment variables the spec names, never from the file.

Deploy then runs as a generated playbook under the harness: approvals apply, every mutation has a content-hash key so deploying twice changes nothing, the task credential carries only the scopes needed, and an interrupted deploy resumes where it stopped.

options: A required email field named email

practice.intro: Write parse_fields(text): split a shorthand like 'email:email!, note:text' by commas; return [name, type, required] for each (required is True if the type ends with '!'; strip spaces; the type has no '!').

practice.intro: Write page_file(path): '/' becomes 'index.html'; '/pricing' becomes 'pricing/index.html'; '/work/a' becomes 'work/a/index.html'.

practice.intro: Write merge_by_name(base, override): both are lists of [name, value] pairs. The result has every name once, in base order, then new names in override order; a name present in both takes the override value.

practice.intro: Write merge_pages(template_pages, spec_pages): lists of [path, title]; spec pages replace template pages with the same path; others keep template order, then new spec pages are appended.

practice.title: Collection rule words
practice.intro: Write rule_meaning(rule): 'open' for 'anyone'; 'signed-in' for 'users'; 'owner' for 'owner'; 'superuser' for 'admin'; otherwise 'custom'.
practice.solution:
def rule_meaning(rule):
    return {'anyone': 'open', 'users': 'signed-in', 'owner': 'owner', 'admin': 'superuser'}.get(rule, 'custom')

practice.title: Collection deploy calls
practice.intro: Write collection_calls(existing, wanted): for each wanted collection name in order return 'collection_update:NAME' if it is in existing else 'collection_create:NAME'.
practice.solution:
def collection_calls(existing, wanted):
    return [('collection_update:' if w in existing else 'collection_create:') + w for w in wanted]

practice.title: Secrets by name only
practice.intro: Write secret_refs(spec_keys): spec_keys is a list of [key, value] pairs from a backend entry; return the sorted keys that end with '_env' (they name environment variables), and nothing from the values.
practice.hint: A spec names variables, never values.
practice.solution:
def secret_refs(spec_keys):
    return sorted([k for k, v in spec_keys if k.endswith('_env')])

chapters.title: Every surface: CLI, REPL, MCP, HTTP and Python, and working with agents

maps.title: Surfaces
links: Agent | needs | A person for secrets

summary: Every capability is a command in one registry, reachable the same way everywhere: the command line, an interactive REPL (or JSON lines for programs), an MCP server over stdio, a local HTTP server and the Python SDK. Results are the same JSON values.

A command named site.build is jade site build on the CLI, site.build in JSON lines, site_build over MCP and POST /v1/commands/site.build over HTTP. jade commands lists them all with parameters as data.
Agents can do nearly everything except widen their own permissions: approvals, secrets, playbook approval and deploy confirmation need a person at a terminal.

glossary.def: The single list of commands from which every surface is generated.
The standard result object with schema jade.v1, an ok flag, the command and the data or error.
A protocol of one request per line in and one answer per line out, with an id.
A process exposing the commands as tools over the Model Context Protocol.
The local-only address 127.0.0.1; other hosts need a token.

items: ELI5. Write three lines, a name, a sentence and a style, and a machine builds a whole website with its back room already set up.

One list of commands, many doors. That is the design. Instead of writing a command line, then an HTTP API, then a tool server, then SDK wrappers, each by hand and each slightly different, the toolkit has a registry. Each entry has a name like site.build, parameters and a function.
Surfaces are generated from it, so a capability appears everywhere at once and behaves the same.

On the command line you run jade site build with a json flag to get a stable envelope: schema jade.v1, ok true, the command, and data, or ok false with an error carrying code, message and remediation. The REPL lets you type commands without the word jade, with arguments as values then key=value.
For programs, the JSON lines mode reads one request per line, each with an id, a command and args, and writes one answer per line, so many calls can share one process.

The MCP surface turns commands into tools whose names use underscores, such as site_build, site_plan, site_deploy, playbook_run and docs_search, so an agent in any MCP client can use them. Nothing asks a person there, so the approvals in the config decide and playbooks must be approved beforehand.

The HTTP surface, jade serve, listens on loopback; any other host needs a bearer token in the header, and tokens in URLs are refused. Routes list playbooks, run them, call any command and browse the docs.
From Python you import jade, build a Site, load a Stack and run commands, with asyncio wrappers too.

What may an agent not do? It must not widen its own permissions. Over MCP, HTTP and JSON lines, changing approvals, target URLs, secret storage options or legacy acceptance, storing or deleting secrets, approving a playbook, and deploying with yes are refused with JADE302 and need a person.

Everything else an agent can do, including running the init wizard from an answers file. One honest caveat in the docs: this guard holds on those surfaces. An agent with a shell running as you can do what you can, so run agents as a user with less.
The recipes for agents are short: start from a template, list sections before guessing parameters, plan before deploy, and treat JADE103 or JADE30x as stop signs.

chapters.title: Security: threats, defences and responsible use

maps.title: Security
links: Run agents | as a lesser user | Contain the shell

summary: The threat model assumes agents can be fooled. A malicious note, web page or MCP server can carry instructions that steer an agent. The defence is not hoping the agent resists; it is limiting what a steered agent can do: approvals, narrow scopes, short credentials and an audit log it cannot edit.

The toolkit adds header-only auth, keyring secrets, redaction of output, hashed playbook approvals, a sandboxed expression language and escaped page output. Treat data from targets as data, never as instructions.
Some Base scopes, schema, hooks and settings, are close to root and should be granted sparingly. Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub security advisories.

glossary.def: Text in data an agent reads that tries to give the agent new instructions.
Giving a task only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs.
Removing secrets from output, logs and errors.
Leaking data out of a system, for example through a tool call to a hostile server.
Using several independent protections so that one failure is not fatal.

keyPoints: Assume the agent can be steered.
Bound the blast radius: scopes, TTL, approvals.

items: ELI5. One list of things the system can do, shown on a phone, a keyboard, a robot's plug and a web door, all with the same names. A robot cannot give itself more permission.

Security for agents differs from security for ordinary programs in one important way: the program can be talked into things. An agent reads notes, web pages and tool results as part of its job, and any of them may contain text written by an attacker that reads like an instruction.

A model cannot reliably tell the difference between its owner's request and a request embedded in a document. So the sensible design assumes that sooner or later an agent will be steered, and arranges for the damage to be small.

The documentation sets out a table of threats. A malicious note in Vault, a hostile web page or a rogue MCP server might steer the agent; what limits it is Vault's approvals, Base scopes and short task credentials, and the audit log that records every call and refusal.

A stolen Vault token is not a Base token, and a task credential expires in minutes. A compromised Base might return false data or text that tries to steer Vault's agent, so results are treated as data and approvals still apply.
A leaked config exposes only URLs and approval rules, because it holds no secrets by design.

lesson.code:
# defence in depth, as configuration
approvals:
  base.read: ["*"]
  base.write: ["record_create:feedback"]    # one collection only
  base.schema: {deny: ["*"]}              # no schema changes at all
  http_request: {allow_hosts: [api.example.com], deny_hosts: ["*"]}
targets:
  base: {credentials: {ttl: 5m}}            # shorter than the default

items: Several smaller protections add up. Authorization headers never appear in URLs, so they never reach logs. Verbose mode redacts them and any registered secret. Generated pages escape all text, and markdown drops raw HTML and javascript links, so site content cannot inject script.

The expression language has no calls, imports or I/O, so a template cannot run code. Playbook approval is bound to a file hash, so a swapped file is not trusted. Idempotency keys stop a replayed or retried request from doing a mutation twice.

Judgement still matters. The scopes schema, hooks and settings let a holder change structure, run server code or alter configuration, which is close to full control, so give them sparingly and prefer scoping a task to read and write.

Run agents as an operating-system user with little access, because the guards cover the toolkit's surfaces and not a shell. Keep a person in the loop for irreversible actions. Read the audit log, since a log nobody reads protects nobody.
And if you find a vulnerability, report it privately through the security advisories of the repository concerned, not in a public issue.

practice.title: Match the defence
practice.intro: Pair each defence with the threat it addresses.

practice.title: Redact secrets
practice.intro: Write redact(text, secrets): replace every occurrence of each secret in text with '***'. Longer secrets first.

practice.title: Escape HTML
practice.intro: Write escape(text): replace & with &, < with <, > with >, and " with " (ampersand first).
practice.solution:
def escape(text):
    return text.replace('&', '&').replace('<', '<').replace('>', '>').replace('"', '"')

practice.title: Safe link
practice.intro: Write safe_link(url): False if the URL, lower-cased and stripped of leading spaces, starts with 'javascript:', 'data:' or 'vbscript:'; otherwise True.

practice.title: Root-like scopes
practice.intro: Write risky(scopes): the sorted list of requested scopes that are 'schema', 'hooks' or 'settings'.
practice.solution:
def risky(scopes):
    return sorted([s for s in set(scopes) if s in ('schema', 'hooks', 'settings')])

practice.title: Host allow-list
practice.intro: Write host_ok(host, allow_hosts, deny_hosts): False if a deny pattern matches ('*' matches everything, otherwise exact match); True if the host is in allow_hosts; otherwise False. Allow beats the catch-all deny only if the host is explicitly allowed; a specific deny always wins.

practice.title: Blast radius
practice.intro: Write blast_radius(scopes, ttl_minutes): a risk score = (number of scopes) x ttl_minutes, plus 100 for each of schema, hooks or settings among the scopes.

practice.title: Instruction or data
practice.intro: Write looks_like_injection(text): True if the lower-cased text contains 'ignore previous instructions', 'ignore all previous', or 'you must now'. (A crude filter, which is not a defence on its own.)
